What it shows.

  • Privacy separates the two groups most: 62% of those who want stronger action raise it, against 27% of the rest (V = 0.34, a medium effect). Fairness (58% vs 29%, V = 0.28) and unequal pricing (57% vs 34%, V = 0.22) follow.
  • Transparency differs only slightly (12% vs 7%, V = 0.07).
  • Competition and "other" do not differ significantly (p = 0.16 and 0.14).
  • So what: people calling for a ban are driven mainly by the use of their personal data. That is the concern a disclosure-only rule does least to address.

10. Governance checks¶

The thresholds fixed at the start of Section 8 are applied here. Each check passes or fails; failures decide what goes to human review and whether results may be reported automatically. Section 12 then back-tests the review rules, checks subgroup disparity and harm at scale, maps every failure mode to a safeguard and scores each risk; the governance memo sets out the full rules and escalation path.

In [39]:
# GOVERNANCE CHECKS AND HUMAN-REVIEW QUEUE
# Applies every threshold fixed at the start of Section 8 and records pass or
# fail. If any check fails, results may not be reported automatically: they
# are reported only together with human review of the flagged comments.

if labels_all is None or gold is None:
    print("PENDING: governance checks need the hand-coded gold standard (Section 8).")
else:
    # 1. Gather the evidence for each check
    sc = stance_scores.set_index("model").loc[BEST]                      # stance scores of the chosen Claude version
    rs = reason_scores.set_index("model").loc[BEST]                      # reason scores of the chosen Claude version
    pc = stance_per_class[(stance_per_class["model"] == BEST) & (stance_per_class["gold_examples"] >= THRESHOLDS["min_class_support"])]
    invalid = ((labels_all["stance"] == "INVALID") | labels_all["parse_error"] | labels_all["invalid_reason_label"]).mean()

    # 2. Each check: name, measured value, rule (>= or <=), threshold
    checks = [
        ("Human stance kappa", human_stance["kappa"].iloc[0], ">=", THRESHOLDS["min_human_kappa"]),
        ("Claude stance macro-F1 (judged stances)", sc["macro_f1"], ">=", THRESHOLDS["min_stance_macro_f1"]),
        ("Lowest stance recall (categories with >= 5 gold)", pc["recall"].min(), ">=", THRESHOLDS["min_stance_class_recall"]),
        ("Claude reason micro-F1", rs["micro_f1"], ">=", THRESHOLDS["min_reason_micro_f1"]),
        ("Stance stability across 3 runs", stability, ">=", THRESHOLDS["min_stability"]),
        ("Worst length-group error ratio", length_slices.loc[length_slices["comments"] >= 10, "ratio_vs_best"].max(), "<=",
         THRESHOLDS["max_length_error_ratio"]),
        ("Low-confidence share (production)", (labels_all["confidence"] == "low").mean(), "<=", THRESHOLDS["max_low_confidence_share"]),
        ("Invalid-answer share (production)", invalid, "<=", THRESHOLDS["max_invalid_share"]),
        ("Evidence quote found in comment (production)", labels_all["quote_found"].mean(), ">=", THRESHOLDS["min_quote_found_share"]),
    ]
    governance = pd.DataFrame(checks, columns=["check", "value", "rule", "threshold"])
    governance["passed"] = np.where(governance["rule"] == ">=", governance["value"] >= governance["threshold"],
                                    governance["value"] <= governance["threshold"])
    governance["value"] = governance["value"].astype(float).round(3)
    display(governance)
    print(f"Checks passed: {governance['passed'].sum()} of {len(governance)}")
    print("Automatic reporting allowed:", "YES" if governance["passed"].all() else
          "NO - results are reported only with human review of the queue below")

    # 3. Chart: each check as pass (green) or fail (red), for the slides and memo
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
    g = governance.iloc[::-1]
    ax.barh(g["check"], [1] * len(g), color=["#55A868" if p else "#C44E52" for p in g["passed"]])
    for i, r in enumerate(g.itertuples()):
        ax.text(0.02, i, f"{'PASS' if r.passed else 'FAIL'}   {r.value:g} {r.rule} {r.threshold:g}",
                va="center", fontsize=8, color="white", fontweight="bold")
    ax.set(xlim=(0, 1), xticks=[], title=f"Governance checks: {governance['passed'].sum()} of {len(governance)} passed")
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=8)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(FIG / "governance_checks.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()

    # 4. Human-review queue: every comment with low confidence, an invalid answer,
    # or a quote that was not found in the comment (a sign the answer may be made up)
    flags = pd.DataFrame({"low confidence": labels_all["confidence"] == "low",
                          "invalid answer": (labels_all["stance"] == "INVALID") | labels_all["parse_error"] | labels_all["invalid_reason_label"],
                          "quote not found": ~labels_all["quote_found"]})
    review = labels_all[flags.any(axis=1)].copy()
    review["reason_for_review"] = flags[flags.any(axis=1)].apply(lambda r: "; ".join(r.index[r]), axis=1)
    review[["comment_id", "reason_for_review", "stance", "confidence", "evidence_quote"]].to_csv(CODING / "human_review_queue.csv", index=False)

    # 5. Random audit: 5% of all comments, drawn even when every check passes,
    # so a person keeps checking the model over time
    audit = labels_all.sample(frac=THRESHOLDS["audit_share"], random_state=SEED)
    audit[["comment_id", "stance", "evidence_quote"]].assign(reasons=audit["reasons"].map(reasons_to_text)).to_csv(
        CODING / "audit_sample.csv", index=False)
    print(f"Human-review queue: {len(review)} comments ({len(review) / len(labels_all):.1%}) -> coding/human_review_queue.csv")
    print(flags.sum().to_string())
    print(f"Random audit: {len(audit)} comments ({THRESHOLDS['audit_share']:.0%}) -> coding/audit_sample.csv")

What it shows.

  • 8 of 9 checks pass. The one failure is length: long comments are wrong 5.8 times as often as short ones, against a limit of 1.25×. Under our own rule, results are therefore reported only together with human review of the flagged comments.
  • Two passes are on the edge: stability is exactly at 90%, and quotes are found in 95.3% of comments against a 95% threshold. Both need watching on the next run.
  • The review queue holds 256 comments (16.3%): 188 with low confidence and 73 whose quote was not found (5 are both), plus a random audit of 78 comments (5%).
  • Section 12 tests whether this queue actually catches Claude's errors.

11. Cost analysis¶

Costs are measured from the token counts logged with every API call. The comparison with human coding uses an estimate of the coders' time, worked out from the length of the 80 gold comments (we did not time ourselves).

In [40]:
# COST: MEASURED LLM COST AND PROJECTION VS HUMAN CODING
# Every Claude call was logged with its tokens and time (Section 7.5), so cost
# and speed are measured, not estimated. They are compared with the time the
# coders actually spent labeling comments by hand.

# 1. Human-side time and cost (estimated; state these assumptions in the report)
# We did not time ourselves, so human coding time is estimated from the
# length of the 80 gold comments: time to read each comment carefully, plus
# time to choose a stance and tick the reasons. Reconciliation is not included,
# so this is a conservative (low) estimate of the human cost.
READING_WPM = 200                # careful reading speed, words per minute
DECISION_SECONDS = 30            # time to pick a stance and tick reasons for one comment
HUMAN_HOURLY_RATE = 30.0         # USD per hour for an analyst (assumption)

gold_words = df.loc[df["comment_id"].isin(gold_ids), "n_words"]       # word count of each gold comment
HUMAN_MINUTES_FOR_GOLD = (gold_words.sum() / READING_WPM * 60 + DECISION_SECONDS * len(gold_words)) / 60
print(f"Estimated human coding time for the {len(gold_words)} gold comments: {HUMAN_MINUTES_FOR_GOLD:.0f} minutes per coder "
      f"({gold_words.sum():,} words at {READING_WPM} words per minute + {DECISION_SECONDS} seconds per comment)")

# 2. Load every logged Claude call and price it
log_files = list(LLM_DIR.glob("labels_*.jsonl"))
assert log_files, "No LLM calls logged yet: run Section 7.5 first"
logs = pd.concat([pd.read_json(p, lines=True) for p in log_files], ignore_index=True)
assert (logs["input_tokens"] > 0).all() and (logs["output_tokens"] > 0).all(), "Missing token counts"
logs["cost_usd"] = (logs["input_tokens"] * PRICE_IN_PER_MTOK + logs["output_tokens"] * PRICE_OUT_PER_MTOK) / 1e6

# 3. Cost and speed per run (smoke test, zero-shot, few-shot, stability reruns)
per_variant = logs.groupby("variant").agg(calls=("comment_id", "size"), mean_input_tokens=("input_tokens", "mean"),
                                          mean_output_tokens=("output_tokens", "mean"),
                                          cost_per_comment=("cost_usd", "mean"), total_cost=("cost_usd", "sum"),
                                          total_minutes=("latency_s", lambda s: s.sum() / 60),
                                          median_seconds=("latency_s", "median"))
display(per_variant.round(5))
print(f"Total spent on the API in this project: ${logs['cost_usd'].sum():.4f}")

# 4. Per-comment cost and time of the version used in production, vs humans
production_variant = BEST_VARIANT if gold is not None else "zeroshot"
llm_cost_per_comment = logs.loc[logs["variant"] == production_variant, "cost_usd"].mean()
llm_seconds_per_comment = logs.loc[logs["variant"] == production_variant, "latency_s"].mean()
human_seconds_per_comment = HUMAN_MINUTES_FOR_GOLD * 60 / N_GOLD
print(f"Claude ({production_variant}): ${llm_cost_per_comment:.5f} and {llm_seconds_per_comment:.1f} seconds per comment | "
      f"humans: {human_seconds_per_comment:.0f} seconds per comment")

# 5. Projection to larger dockets: cost and time, Claude vs humans.
# 'llm_plus_review' adds a person auditing 5% of comments (governance rule).
# Claude time assumes one comment at a time, as in this notebook; sending
# comments in parallel would be much faster.
projection = pd.DataFrame({"comments": [1_000, 10_000, 100_000]})
projection["llm_cost_usd"] = projection["comments"] * llm_cost_per_comment
projection["llm_hours"] = projection["comments"] * llm_seconds_per_comment / 3600
projection["human_hours"] = projection["comments"] * human_seconds_per_comment / 3600
projection["human_cost_usd"] = projection["human_hours"] * HUMAN_HOURLY_RATE
projection["llm_plus_review_usd"] = projection["llm_cost_usd"] + projection["human_cost_usd"] * THRESHOLDS["audit_share"]
display(projection.round(2))

# 6. Chart: projected cost on a log scale (the gap is too large for a normal scale)
plot = projection.melt(id_vars="comments", value_vars=["llm_cost_usd", "llm_plus_review_usd", "human_cost_usd"],
                       var_name="approach", value_name="usd")
plot["approach"] = plot["approach"].map({"llm_cost_usd": "Claude only", "llm_plus_review_usd": "Claude + 5% human audit",
                                         "human_cost_usd": "Human coding only"})
plot["comments"] = plot["comments"].map(lambda n: f"{n:,}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.8))
sns.barplot(data=plot, x="comments", y="usd", hue="approach", palette=["#4C72B0", "#8172B3", "#B0B0B0"], ax=ax)
ax.set_yscale("log")
for cont in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(cont, labels=[f"${v:,.0f}" if v >= 1 else f"${v:.2f}" for v in cont.datavalues], fontsize=7, padding=2)
ax.set(title="Projected cost of labeling comments", xlabel="Number of comments", ylabel="US dollars (log scale)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(FIG / "cost_projection.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

How to read this chart. Projected cost of labelling 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 comments three ways, on a log scale (each gridline is ten times the one below).

What it shows.

  • Claude is cheap to run: $0.44 for all 1,566 comments, $0.28 per 1,000. At 100,000 comments: about $28 with Claude alone, $1,985 with the 5% human audit, and about $39,000 (1,305 hours) by hand.
  • Even generous human review stays far cheaper than hand coding: reviewing the full 16% queue for 100,000 comments would take about 214 hours (about $6,400).
  • Claude's time is not free either: 1.7 seconds per comment, one at a time, is about 46 hours for 100,000 comments; sending comments in parallel would cut this sharply.
  • So what: the real cost of the workflow is building and re-checking the gold standard, not running the model.

12. Governance in depth: back-tests, disparity, harm and safeguards¶

Section 10 applied the thresholds. This section tests whether the rules built on those thresholds actually work on our data, following the Class 16 and Class 18 methods, and gives the evidence the governance memo needs under each rule:

  • 12.1 Back-tests: for each human-review rule, how many comments it flags and how many of Claude's real errors it catches, plus how sensitive it is to the threshold.
  • 12.2 Subgroup disparity: whether Claude is worse for some kinds of comments (disparate-impact ratio, chi-square on error rates, recall by subgroup).
  • 12.3 Harm at production scale: what the error rate means at 5,000 comments a month, in errors and dollars.
  • 12.4 Safeguard map: every failure mode with its safeguard, a measurable threshold, who acts and which layer.
  • 12.5 Quantitative risk matrix: likelihood × impact for each risk, with likelihood measured from our data where possible.
  • 12.6 Audit trail and shelf life: what every run records, what it cannot record, and when the evaluation expires.
  • 12.7 Governance recommendations and limitations.

All of it uses results already computed: no new labels and no new API calls.

12.1 Back-testing the human-review rules¶

A rule such as "review when confidence is low" is only useful if it fires on a manageable share of comments and catches the errors we care about. Each rule is tested on the 100 hand-coded comments from Section 8.5, where we know which of Claude's stance labels are wrong, and then applied to all 1,566 comments to show the workload it would create.

In [41]:
# BACK-TEST THE HUMAN-REVIEW RULES (Class 18 method)
# For each rule: how many comments it flags and how many of Claude's real
# stance errors it catches (on the hand-coded comments), and how much work
# it would create on all comments.

if gold is None or labels_all is None:
    print("Needs the gold standard (Section 8) and the production run (Section 9).")
else:
    # 1. Evaluation data from Section 8.5: one row per hand-coded comment with Claude's answer
    bt = ev.copy()
    bt["is_error"] = bt["stance_human"] != bt["stance_claude"]
    n_err = int(bt["is_error"].sum())
    LONG_WORDS = 50                                   # the 'long' cut-off used in Section 8.8
    prod = labels_all.copy()                          # all 1,566 production labels (Section 9)

    MAX_WORKLOAD = 0.30                               # Class 18: flagging more than 30% of volume is more than reviewers can handle

    # 2. The rules, written once so they can be applied to any table of labels
    def rule_flags(t, long_words=LONG_WORDS, conf_levels=("low",)):
        low = t["confidence"].isin(conf_levels)
        nf = ~t["quote_found"].astype(bool)
        long_ = t["n_words"] > long_words
        return {"R1 Low confidence": low,
                "R2 Quote not found in the comment": nf,
                "R3 Long comment": long_,
                "Current queue (R1 or R2)": low | nf,
                "Recommended queue (R1 or R2 or R3)": low | nf | long_}

    # 3. Choose the length cut-off for R3: the one whose combined queue catches the most
    # errors while flagging at most 30% of all comments (ties go to the lighter workload)
    choices = []
    for w in [50, 75, 100, 150, 200]:
        f = rule_flags(bt, long_words=w)["Recommended queue (R1 or R2 or R3)"]
        pf = rule_flags(prod, long_words=w)["Recommended queue (R1 or R2 or R3)"]
        choices.append({"long_words": w, "errors_caught": int((f & bt["is_error"]).sum()), "production_flag_rate": pf.mean()})
    choices = pd.DataFrame(choices)
    ok = choices[choices["production_flag_rate"] <= MAX_WORKLOAD]
    REC_WORDS = int((ok if len(ok) else choices).sort_values(["errors_caught", "production_flag_rate"], ascending=[False, True]).iloc[0]["long_words"])
    print("Length cut-off for R3, by errors caught and workload:")
    display(choices.round(3))
    print(f"Chosen: comments over {REC_WORDS} words (most errors caught with at most {MAX_WORKLOAD:.0%} of comments flagged)\n")

    # 4. Back-test: flag rate and errors caught on the hand-coded comments, and the
    # flag rate on all comments (the review workload in production)
    rows = []
    for (name, flag), prod_flag in zip(rule_flags(bt, REC_WORDS).items(), rule_flags(prod, REC_WORDS).values()):
        name = name.replace("R3 Long comment", f"R3 Long comment (over {REC_WORDS} words)")
        caught = int((flag & bt["is_error"]).sum())
        rows.append({"rule": name, "flagged": int(flag.sum()), "flag_rate": flag.mean(), "errors_caught": caught,
                     "catch_rate": caught / n_err, "errors_missed": n_err - caught, "production_flag_rate": prod_flag.mean()})
    backtest = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    print(f"Hand-coded comments: {len(bt)} | Claude stance errors: {n_err} ({n_err / len(bt):.0%})")
    display(backtest.round(3))

    # 5. The warnings from the Class 18 notebook, applied to each rule
    for r in backtest.itertuples():
        notes = []
        if r.production_flag_rate > 0.30: notes.append("flags over 30% of volume: can reviewers keep up?")
        if r.production_flag_rate < 0.02: notes.append("flags almost nothing: may be decorative")
        if r.catch_rate < 0.50: notes.append("misses most errors: needs a second safeguard")
        print(f"- {r.rule}: {'; '.join(notes) if notes else 'workload and catch rate both acceptable'}")

    # 6. Memo-ready back-test lines (one under each rule in the governance memo)
    print("\nBack-test lines for the memo:")
    for r in backtest.itertuples():
        print(f"  {r.rule}: on our {len(bt)} hand-coded comments this rule flags {r.flag_rate:.0%} and catches "
              f"{r.errors_caught} of {n_err} errors; on all comments it would flag {r.production_flag_rate:.1%}.")

    # 7. What the 5% random audit adds: it re-checks a random 5% of the comments the queue
    # does NOT flag, so it is expected to find about 5% of the errors the queue misses
    missed_by_queue = backtest.set_index("rule").loc["Recommended queue (R1 or R2 or R3)", "errors_missed"]
    print(f"\n5% random audit: expected to find {THRESHOLDS['audit_share'] * missed_by_queue:.1f} of the "
          f"{missed_by_queue} errors the recommended queue misses; its main job is to detect drift, not to catch every error.")

    # 8. Sensitivity: does a small change to a threshold swing the result?
    sens = []
    for label, levels in [("confidence low", ("low",)), ("confidence low or medium", ("low", "medium"))]:
        f, pf = rule_flags(bt, conf_levels=levels)["R1 Low confidence"], rule_flags(prod, conf_levels=levels)["R1 Low confidence"]
        sens.append({"setting": label, "flag_rate": f.mean(), "errors_caught": int((f & bt["is_error"]).sum()), "production_flag_rate": pf.mean()})
    for w in [30, 50, 100, 150]:
        f, pf = bt["n_words"] > w, prod["n_words"] > w
        sens.append({"setting": f"long comment > {w} words", "flag_rate": f.mean(), "errors_caught": int((f & bt["is_error"]).sum()),
                     "production_flag_rate": pf.mean()})
    sens = pd.DataFrame(sens)
    sens["catch_rate"] = sens["errors_caught"] / n_err
    display(sens.round(3))

    # 9. Chart: workload (share flagged in production) vs errors caught, one dot per rule
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
    ax.axhspan(0.5, 1.05, xmin=0, xmax=1, color="#EAF4EC", zorder=0)            # catches at least half the errors
    ax.axvspan(MAX_WORKLOAD, 1.0, color="#FBEAEC", zorder=0)                            # flags more than 30% of volume
    short_names = ["R1", "R2", "R3", "Current", "Recommended"]          # short labels on the dots; full names in the legend
    for k, r in enumerate(backtest.itertuples()):
        big = r.rule.startswith(("Current", "Recommended"))
        ax.scatter(r.production_flag_rate, r.catch_rate, s=170 if big else 90, color="#C44E52" if big else "#4C72B0", zorder=3,
                   label=r.rule)
        ax.annotate(short_names[k], (r.production_flag_rate, r.catch_rate), xytext=(8, 8 if k % 2 else -14),
                    textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")
    ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.14), ncol=2, fontsize=8, frameon=False)
    ax.set(xlim=(0, max(0.6, backtest["production_flag_rate"].max() + 0.1)), ylim=(0, 1.05),
           xlabel="Share of all comments flagged for review (workload)", ylabel=f"Share of the {n_err} known errors caught",
           title="Back-test: each review rule's workload vs the errors it catches")
    ax.text(0.31, 0.03, "too much work (>30%)", fontsize=8, color="#9B0C24")
    ax.text(0.005, 0.97, "catches at least half the errors", fontsize=8, color="#1F6B41", va="top")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(FIG / "governance_backtest.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()

How to read this. In the chart, each dot is a review rule: left to right is the share of all comments it would send to a person (the workload), bottom to top is the share of Claude's known stance errors it catches. The best rules sit top-left: little work, most errors caught. The red zone means more than 30% of volume, more than a review team can usually handle; the green zone means the rule catches at least half the errors. The sensitivity table shows how the result moves when a threshold changes.

What it shows.

  • Low confidence alone (R1) is not enough. It flags 12% of all comments but catches only 4 of the 10 errors on the hand-coded comments. Under the Class 18 rule, a rule that misses most errors needs a second safeguard.
  • The cut-off for long comments matters. Adding every comment over 50 words would catch 7 of the 10 errors but send 43% of all comments to people, far above what a review team can handle. Cut-offs of 100, 150 and 200 words all catch 5, so the notebook picks 200 words, the lightest workload.
  • The recommended queue (R1 or R2 or over 200 words) catches 5 of 10 errors (50%) while flagging 21% of all comments, against 4 of 10 for 16% with the current queue. It is the only rule that passes both Class 18 tests, and only just.
  • Confidence is the strongest lever, but expensive. Reviewing low and medium confidence would catch 9 of 10 errors but flag 56% of comments. A cheaper rule worth testing next: review medium-confidence answers only for comments that mention the FTC or the rule, the hardest type of comment (27% wrong, Section 8.9).
  • The 5% random audit is not an error catcher. It is expected to find well under one of the 5 errors the queue misses; its job is to detect drift in comments nobody else reads.
  • Caveat: the back-test rests on 10 known errors, so each caught error moves the catch rate by 10 points. The direction is reliable; the exact percentages are not.

12.2 Subgroup disparity: is Claude worse for some kinds of comments?¶

Overall accuracy can hide a group the model serves badly (Class 16: "80% overall can be 90% for the majority and 60% for a minority"). Our comments have no demographic fields, so the subgroups are types of comment: by length, and by whether the comment talks about the FTC's rule itself. Three checks from Class 16:

  • Disparate-impact ratio (the 1.25× rule): a group's error rate divided by the best group's. Above 1.25 is flagged.
  • Chi-square on error rates: could the differences between groups be chance?
  • Equalized odds: is recall for each main stance similar across groups? A spread above 0.20 is unequal.

A group needs at least 30 comments before its rate is trusted (Class 18 minimum sample size).

In [42]:
# SUBGROUP DISPARITY (Class 16 method)
# Error rates, disparate-impact ratios, a chi-square test and recall by
# subgroup, on the hand-coded comments.

if gold is None or labels_all is None:
    print("Needs the gold standard (Section 8) and the production run (Section 9).")
else:
    MIN_N = 30                      # minimum comments before a group's error rate is trusted

    # 1. Two kinds of subgroup: comment length, and whether the comment talks about the rule itself
    bt["length_group"] = pd.cut(bt["n_words"], bins=[0, 15, 50, np.inf], labels=["short (<=15)", "medium (16-50)", "long (>50)"])
    bt["mentions_rule"] = np.where(bt["text"].str.contains(r"\b(?:ftc|commission|rule|proposal|proposed|regulat\w*)\b", case=False, regex=True),
                                   "mentions the FTC / rule", "does not mention it")

    def disparity(group_col):
        """Error rate, disparate-impact ratio and chi-square test for one way of grouping comments."""
        t = bt.groupby(group_col, observed=True).agg(comments=("is_error", "size"), errors=("is_error", "sum"))
        t["error_rate"] = t["errors"] / t["comments"]
        best = t["error_rate"].min()
        t["ratio_vs_best"] = t["error_rate"] / best if best > 0 else np.nan     # undefined when the best group has no errors
        t["flag_over_1.25"] = t["ratio_vs_best"] > THRESHOLDS["max_length_error_ratio"]
        t["enough_data"] = t["comments"] >= MIN_N
        chi2, p, _, expected = chi2_contingency(pd.crosstab(bt[group_col], bt["is_error"]))
        return t, p, expected.min()

    disp_rows = []
    for col, title in [("length_group", "Comment length"), ("mentions_rule", "Talks about the FTC's rule")]:
        t, p, min_exp = disparity(col)
        print(f"\n{title}: chi-square p = {p:.3f} (smallest expected count {min_exp:.1f}; below 5 makes the test approximate)")
        display(t.round(3))
        disp_rows.append((title, t, p))

    # 2. Equalized odds: recall of the two main stances within each length group
    recall_rows = []
    for g, sub in bt.groupby("length_group", observed=True):
        for s in ["stronger_action", "unclear"]:
            truth = sub["stance_human"] == s
            if truth.sum():
                recall_rows.append({"length_group": g, "stance": s, "comments": int(truth.sum()),
                                    "recall": (truth & (sub["stance_claude"] == s)).sum() / truth.sum()})
    recall_by_group = pd.DataFrame(recall_rows).pivot(index="stance", columns="length_group", values="recall")
    recall_by_group = recall_by_group[[g for g in ["short (<=15)", "medium (16-50)", "long (>50)"] if g in recall_by_group.columns]]
    recall_by_group["spread"] = recall_by_group.max(axis=1) - recall_by_group.min(axis=1)
    recall_by_group["unequal_(>0.20)"] = recall_by_group["spread"] > 0.20
    print("\nEqualized odds: recall of each main stance by length group")
    display(recall_by_group.round(3))

    # 3. Chart: error rate by subgroup with the 1.25x line, and recall by length group
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.2))
    t = disp_rows[0][1]
    best = t["error_rate"].min()
    axes[0].bar(t.index.astype(str), t["error_rate"] * 100, color=["#C44E52" if f else "#B0B0B0" for f in t["flag_over_1.25"]])
    if best > 0:
        axes[0].axhline(best * THRESHOLDS["max_length_error_ratio"] * 100, color="#555555", ls="--", lw=1)
        axes[0].text(-0.4, best * THRESHOLDS["max_length_error_ratio"] * 100 + 0.5, "1.25 x best group", fontsize=8)
    for i, r in enumerate(t.itertuples()):
        axes[0].text(i, r.error_rate * 100 + 0.6, f"{r.error_rate:.0%}\n(n={r.comments})", ha="center", fontsize=9)
    axes[0].set(title=f"Stance error rate by length (chi-square p = {disp_rows[0][2]:.2f})", ylabel="Error rate (%)",
                ylim=(0, t["error_rate"].max() * 140))
    rb = recall_by_group.drop(columns=["spread", "unequal_(>0.20)"])
    x = np.arange(len(rb.columns))
    for k, (s, col) in enumerate(zip(rb.index, ["#C44E52", "#4C72B0"])):
        axes[1].bar(x + (k - 0.5) * 0.38, rb.loc[s], 0.38, color=col, label=s.replace("_", " ").capitalize())
    axes[1].set_xticks(x, [str(c) for c in rb.columns])
    axes[1].set(title="Equalized odds: recall by length group", ylabel="Recall", ylim=(0, 1.1))
    axes[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="lower left")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(FIG / "governance_subgroups.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()

How to read this. The left chart shows Claude's stance error rate for each length group with the number of comments (n); a red bar is more than 1.25 times the best group's rate (the dashed line). The right chart shows recall for the two main stances in each group: equal bars mean Claude serves each group equally; a gap above 0.20 is unequal. The chi-square p-value says whether the differences could be chance (below 0.05 = unlikely to be chance).

What it shows.

  • Length: a clear gap, but not a proven one. Long comments are wrong 17% of the time against 6% for short ones: 2.7 times the best group, above the 1.25× limit (medium comments, at 1.26×, are borderline). Each length group now has at least 30 comments, but with only 2 to 5 errors per group the chi-square test cannot rule out chance (p = 0.34). We treat length as a risk to control (the R3 review rule), not as a proven effect.
  • Comments about the rule itself show the largest gap: 27% wrong against 7% (3.8×), close to significant (p = 0.06), but based on only 15 comments, below the 30-comment minimum. This is the "oppose the rule" misreading from Section 8.9, and the subgroup to watch most closely.
  • Recall is fairly even across lengths (equalized odds): recall for stronger action varies by only 0.07, and for unclear by 0.18 (0.93 on short comments, 0.75 on long ones), both under the 0.20 limit. The drop for unclear on long comments is the one to watch: Claude gives long, critical comments a position the commenter did not state.
  • Which fairness we chose, and why (Class 16: "make it fair" is underspecified). We use equal error rates across comment types (the disparate-impact ratio), because the harm we want to prevent is that some commenters' views are misreported more often than others'. A long, detailed comment should be read as accurately as a short one.

12.3 Harm at production scale¶

An error rate means little to a manager until it is turned into volume and dollars (Class 16: "error rate > dollar figure"). Below, the measured error rate is projected to 5,000 comments a month (the Class 16 benchmark, and a realistic monthly load for an agency or law firm tracking several dockets). The two dollar assumptions are stated in the code and can be changed.

In [43]:
# HARM AT PRODUCTION SCALE (Class 16 method)
# Turns the measured error rate into monthly errors and dollars, before and
# after the review rules.

if gold is None or labels_all is None:
    print("Needs the gold standard (Section 8) and the production run (Section 9).")
else:
    MONTHLY_VOLUME = 5_000             # comments per month (Class 16 benchmark)
    COST_PER_UNCAUGHT_ERROR = 5.00     # assumption: USD of analyst time to find and fix a misreported comment later (10 min at $30/hour)

    # 1. Monthly errors at the measured stance error rate, with a 95% interval
    err_rate = bt["is_error"].mean()
    lo, hi = proportion_confint(int(bt["is_error"].sum()), len(bt), method="wilson")
    monthly_errors = err_rate * MONTHLY_VOLUME
    print(f"Stance error rate: {err_rate:.0%} (95% CI {lo:.0%}-{hi:.0%}) -> about {monthly_errors:,.0f} misread comments a month "
          f"(range {lo * MONTHLY_VOLUME:,.0f}-{hi * MONTHLY_VOLUME:,.0f})")

    # 2. With the recommended review queue: errors caught by people, errors that slip through
    rec = backtest.set_index("rule").loc["Recommended queue (R1 or R2 or R3)"]
    caught_month = monthly_errors * rec["catch_rate"]
    slip_month = monthly_errors - caught_month
    audit_month = slip_month * THRESHOLDS["audit_share"]
    review_month = rec["production_flag_rate"] * MONTHLY_VOLUME
    review_hours = review_month * human_seconds_per_comment / 3600
    print(f"Recommended queue reviews {review_month:,.0f} comments a month ({review_hours:,.0f} hours, ${review_hours * HUMAN_HOURLY_RATE:,.0f}) "
          f"and catches about {caught_month:,.0f} of the {monthly_errors:,.0f} errors")
    print(f"About {slip_month:,.0f} errors a month slip through (the 5% audit finds about {audit_month:,.1f} of them): "
          f"${slip_month * COST_PER_UNCAUGHT_ERROR:,.0f} a month at ${COST_PER_UNCAUGHT_ERROR:.2f} each")

    # 3. The worst category (Class 16: lowest-quality class x its share x volume)
    limit = stance_all.set_index("stance").loc["limit_or_oppose_intervention"]
    limit_share = (prod["stance"] == "limit_or_oppose_intervention").mean()
    limit_month = limit_share * MONTHLY_VOLUME
    print(f"Worst category: 'limit or oppose' ({limit_share:.1%} of comments, precision {limit['precision']:.2f} on {int(limit['claude_count'])} "
          f"hand-coded cases): about {limit_month:,.0f} comments a month labelled this way, of which about "
          f"{limit_month * (1 - limit['precision']):,.0f} may be wrong, overstating opposition to the FTC")

    # 4. Chart: what happens to 5,000 comments a month
    stages = ["Comments", "Misread by Claude", "Caught by review queue", "Slip through", "Found by 5% audit"]
    values = [MONTHLY_VOLUME, monthly_errors, caught_month, slip_month, audit_month]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.6))
    bars = ax.barh(stages[::-1], values[::-1], color=["#55A868", "#DD8452", "#C44E52", "#4C72B0", "#B0B0B0"][::-1])
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    for b, v in zip(bars, values[::-1]):
        ax.text(v * 1.08, b.get_y() + b.get_height() / 2, f"{v:,.0f}" if v >= 10 else f"{v:,.1f}", va="center", fontsize=9)
    ax.set(title=f"Harm at scale: {MONTHLY_VOLUME:,} comments a month", xlabel="Comments per month (log scale)")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(FIG / "governance_harm_at_scale.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()

Stance error rate: 10% (95% CI 6%-17%) -> about 500 misread comments a month (range 276-872)
Recommended queue reviews 1,047 comments a month (14 hours, $410) and catches about 250 of the 500 errors
About 250 errors a month slip through (the 5% audit finds about 12.5 of them): $1,250 a month at $5.00 each
Worst category: 'limit or oppose' (2.5% of comments, precision 0.20 on 5 hand-coded cases): about 125 comments a month labelled this way, of which about 100 may be wrong, overstating opposition to the FTC

How to read this. The chart follows 5,000 comments through one month: how many Claude misreads, how many of those the review queue sends to a person, how many slip through, and how many the random audit would find. It uses a log scale so the small numbers stay visible.

What it shows. At a 10% error rate, about 500 comments a month would be misread. The recommended queue sends about 1,050 comments a month to a person (about 14 hours of review, roughly $410) and catches about half of the misreads (250); the other 250 slip through, of which the 5% audit would find about 12. The errors that slip through are the real residual risk: they are not costly one by one, but if they are concentrated in one direction (for example, overstating opposition to the FTC) they can bias a report. That is why the "limit or oppose" category is singled out: it is small (about 125 comments a month), but about 100 of those labels may be wrong, so it must never be reported without human review. This budget case (a few hundred misreads a month, a few hours of review) is the argument for keeping a human-review step.

12.4 Safeguard map: every failure mode, one safeguard, one number¶

Class 16's rule: every failure mode needs a safeguard with a quantitative threshold a machine could enforce, a named person who acts, and a layer. The "measured now" column shows where our run stands today.

In [44]:
# SAFEGUARD MAP (Class 16 template)
# One row per failure mode: the safeguard, its measurable threshold, who
# acts, which layer, and the value measured in this run.

if gold is None or labels_all is None:
    print("Needs the gold standard (Section 8) and the production run (Section 9).")
else:
    masked = int((df["text"] != df["text"].map(mask_names)).sum())        # comments where a typed-in name was masked
    best_scores = stance_scores.set_index("model").loc[BEST]               # the chosen Claude version's stance scores
    safeguards = pd.DataFrame([
        {"failure_mode": "Hallucination (invented evidence)", "safeguard": "Quote check: Claude's evidence quote must appear word for word in the comment",
         "threshold": f"Review every comment whose quote is not found; stop the run if under {THRESHOLDS['min_quote_found_share']:.0%} are found",
         "who_acts": "Reviewer; workflow owner stops the run", "layer": "Output check + human review gate",
         "measured_now": f"{prod['quote_found'].mean():.1%} of quotes found"},
        {"failure_mode": "Misclassification", "safeguard": "Gold standard of 100 hand-coded comments; review queue",
         "threshold": f"Stance macro-F1 >= {THRESHOLDS['min_stance_macro_f1']}, reason micro-F1 >= {THRESHOLDS['min_reason_micro_f1']}; review every low-confidence answer",
         "who_acts": "Workflow owner blocks automatic reporting if a score fails", "layer": "Pre-deployment test + human review gate",
         "measured_now": f"stance F1 {best_scores['macro_f1']:.2f}, accuracy {best_scores['accuracy']:.0%}"},
        {"failure_mode": "Bias / disparate impact", "safeguard": "Error rate by comment type (length, mentions the rule)",
         "threshold": f"Flag any group with error rate > {THRESHOLDS['max_length_error_ratio']}x the best group (min {MIN_N} comments); review all long comments",
         "who_acts": "Reviewer reads every long comment; owner re-tests the prompt", "layer": "Monitoring + human review gate",
         "measured_now": f"long comments {length_slices['ratio_vs_best'].max():.1f}x the best group (FAILED)"},
        {"failure_mode": "Privacy leakage", "safeguard": "Names typed into comments are masked before any API call; only comment text is sent; API key kept in .env",
         "threshold": "100% of comments pass through name masking; no fields other than comment text leave the notebook",
         "who_acts": "Workflow owner", "layer": "Input filter (deterministic)",
         "measured_now": f"{masked} comments had a name masked"},
        {"failure_mode": "Automation bias", "safeguard": "Mandatory review queue plus a random audit; reviewers record agree/correct",
         "threshold": f"Review 100% of flagged comments; audit {THRESHOLDS['audit_share']:.0%} of every run; investigate if reviewers agree with Claude > 98% of the time",
         "who_acts": "Second reviewer checks a sample of the first reviewer's decisions", "layer": "Human review gate",
         "measured_now": f"{len(review)} comments queued ({len(review) / len(prod):.0%}), {len(audit)} audited"},
        {"failure_mode": "Context failure (misread proposal)", "safeguard": "Dictionary rule: disliking the practice is not opposition to the FTC; review comments that talk about the rule",
         "threshold": "Never report the 'limit or oppose' share without human review of every comment in it",
         "who_acts": "Reviewer", "layer": "System prompt + human review gate",
         "measured_now": f"'limit or oppose' precision {stance_all.set_index('stance').loc['limit_or_oppose_intervention', 'precision']:.2f}"},
        {"failure_mode": "Evaluation failure / drift", "safeguard": "Re-run the gold-standard evaluation and stability test",
         "threshold": f"On any model or prompt change, or quarterly; investigate if stance F1 drops by more than the MDD ({mdd_single:.2f}) or stability < {THRESHOLDS['min_stability']:.0%}",
         "who_acts": "Workflow owner revalidates before the next run", "layer": "Monitoring",
         "measured_now": f"stability {stability:.0%}, MDD {mdd_single:.2f}"},
        {"failure_mode": "Accountability failure", "safeguard": "Every call logged (model, prompt version, settings, tokens, time, raw answer); review decisions saved",
         "threshold": "Alert if any saved answer lacks model, prompt version or raw answer; block reporting of a run with missing logs",
         "who_acts": "Workflow owner", "layer": "System logging",
         "measured_now": f"{len(logs):,} calls logged"},
    ])
    with pd.option_context("display.max_colwidth", None):
        display(safeguards)
failure_mode safeguard threshold who_acts layer measured_now
0 Hallucination (invented evidence) Quote check: Claude's evidence quote must appear word for word in the comment Review every comment whose quote is not found; stop the run if under 95% are found Reviewer; workflow owner stops the run Output check + human review gate 95.3% of quotes found
1 Misclassification Gold standard of 100 hand-coded comments; review queue Stance macro-F1 >= 0.7, reason micro-F1 >= 0.7; review every low-confidence answer Workflow owner blocks automatic reporting if a score fails Pre-deployment test + human review gate stance F1 0.93, accuracy 90%
2 Bias / disparate impact Error rate by comment type (length, mentions the rule) Flag any group with error rate > 1.25x the best group (min 30 comments); review all long comments Reviewer reads every long comment; owner re-tests the prompt Monitoring + human review gate long comments 5.8x the best group (FAILED)
3 Privacy leakage Names typed into comments are masked before any API call; only comment text is sent; API key kept in .env 100% of comments pass through name masking; no fields other than comment text leave the notebook Workflow owner Input filter (deterministic) 37 comments had a name masked
4 Automation bias Mandatory review queue plus a random audit; reviewers record agree/correct Review 100% of flagged comments; audit 5% of every run; investigate if reviewers agree with Claude > 98% of the time Second reviewer checks a sample of the first reviewer's decisions Human review gate 256 comments queued (16%), 78 audited
5 Context failure (misread proposal) Dictionary rule: disliking the practice is not opposition to the FTC; review comments that talk about the rule Never report the 'limit or oppose' share without human review of every comment in it Reviewer System prompt + human review gate 'limit or oppose' precision 0.20
6 Evaluation failure / drift Re-run the gold-standard evaluation and stability test On any model or prompt change, or quarterly; investigate if stance F1 drops by more than the MDD (0.08) or stability < 90% Workflow owner revalidates before the next run Monitoring stability 90%, MDD 0.08
7 Accountability failure Every call logged (model, prompt version, settings, tokens, time, raw answer); review decisions saved Alert if any saved answer lacks model, prompt version or raw answer; block reporting of a run with missing logs Workflow owner System logging 1,709 calls logged

How to read this table. Each row is one way the workflow can fail. Read it left to right: what goes wrong, what stops it, the number that triggers action, who acts, and where in the workflow the safeguard sits. The last column is today's measured value, so each rule can be checked against our data.

What it shows. Every failure mode has a threshold a machine can check, but the layers are uneven. Hallucination, privacy and accountability are handled by automatic checks (quote matching, name masking, logging). Misclassification, bias, context failure and automation bias all depend on the human review gate, which is why that gate needs a trigger that actually catches errors (12.1). Bias is the one row that fails today. Its safeguard in practice is the length rule chosen in 12.1 (comments over 200 words), and the subgroup with the largest gap, comments about the FTC's rule (12.2), is the next one to target.

12.5 Quantitative risk matrix¶

Each risk is scored for likelihood and impact on a 1–5 scale; the risk score is likelihood × impact (1–6 low, 8–12 medium, 15–25 high). Where our data measures how often the problem happens, likelihood comes from that rate (under 2% = 1, 2–5% = 2, 5–15% = 3, 15–30% = 4, over 30% = 5). Where it cannot be measured, likelihood is the team's judgement and is marked "assumed". Impact is always a judgement, with the reason given.

In [45]:
# QUANTITATIVE RISK MATRIX
# Likelihood from measured rates where possible, impact by team judgement,
# score = likelihood x impact.

if gold is None or labels_all is None:
    print("Needs the gold standard (Section 8) and the production run (Section 9).")
else:
    def likelihood_from_rate(rate):
        """Maps a measured rate to the 1-5 likelihood scale."""
        return 1 if rate < 0.02 else 2 if rate < 0.05 else 3 if rate < 0.15 else 4 if rate < 0.30 else 5

    transp = reason_all.set_index("reason").loc["transparency_disclosure"]
    long_rate = bt.loc[bt["n_words"] > LONG_WORDS, "is_error"].mean()     # error rate on comments over 50 words
    risks = [
        ("Stance misread", bt["is_error"].mean(), 4, "misrepresents what the public asked for"),
        ("'Limit or oppose' overstated", (1 - limit["precision"]) if limit["claude_count"] > 0 else None, 3, "small share, but inflates opposition to the FTC"),
        ("Long comments misread", long_rate, 4, "detailed comments carry the most argument"),
        ("Invented or unsupported quote", 1 - prod["quote_found"].mean(), 3, "evidence shown to readers would be false"),
        ("Transparency arguments missed", 1 - transp["recall"], 3, "understates the disclosure concern, the FTC's main remedy"),
        ("Answer changes between runs", 1 - stability, 2, "results not exactly repeatable"),
        ("Model update changes behaviour", None, 4, "all evaluation numbers silently expire"),
        ("Personal data sent to the API", None, 4, "privacy breach for commenters"),
        ("Reviewers rubber-stamp Claude", None, 3, "human review stops catching errors"),
    ]
    ASSUMED_LIKELIHOOD = {"Model update changes behaviour": 3, "Personal data sent to the API": 1, "Reviewers rubber-stamp Claude": 3,
                          "'Limit or oppose' overstated": 1}      # used only if Claude made no 'limit or oppose' labels
    rm = pd.DataFrame([{"risk": r, "measured_rate": rate, "likelihood": likelihood_from_rate(rate) if rate is not None else ASSUMED_LIKELIHOOD[r],
                        "basis": "measured" if rate is not None else "assumed", "impact": imp, "why_impact": why}
                       for r, rate, imp, why in risks])
    rm["score"] = rm["likelihood"] * rm["impact"]
    rm["level"] = np.where(rm["score"] >= 15, "HIGH", np.where(rm["score"] >= 8, "MEDIUM", "LOW"))
    rm = rm.sort_values("score", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
    rm.index = rm.index + 1                                    # risk numbers used on the chart
    display(rm.round(3))

    # Chart: 5 x 5 grid coloured by score, each risk plotted as its number
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.5))
    grid = np.array([[l * i for l in range(1, 6)] for i in range(1, 6)])
    ax.imshow(grid, origin="lower", cmap="RdYlGn_r", alpha=0.35, extent=(0.5, 5.5, 0.5, 5.5), vmin=1, vmax=25)
    ax.grid(False)                                                     # cell borders drawn below instead of gridlines through the dots
    for v in np.arange(0.5, 6, 1):
        ax.axhline(v, color="white", lw=2)
        ax.axvline(v, color="white", lw=2)
    offsets = {}
    for n, r in rm.iterrows():
        k = offsets.get((r["likelihood"], r["impact"]), 0)
        offsets[(r["likelihood"], r["impact"])] = k + 1
        ax.scatter(r["likelihood"] + (k % 3 - 1) * 0.25, r["impact"] + (k // 3) * 0.25 - 0.1, s=330,
                   color="#1B2A41" if r["basis"] == "measured" else "white", edgecolor="#1B2A41", zorder=3)
        ax.text(r["likelihood"] + (k % 3 - 1) * 0.25, r["impact"] + (k // 3) * 0.25 - 0.1, str(n), ha="center", va="center",
                fontsize=9, color="white" if r["basis"] == "measured" else "#1B2A41", zorder=4)
    ax.set(xticks=range(1, 6), yticks=range(1, 6), xlabel="Likelihood (1 = rare, 5 = frequent)", ylabel="Impact (1 = minor, 5 = severe)",
           title="Risk matrix (filled = likelihood measured, white = assumed)")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(FIG / "governance_risk_matrix.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()
    for n, r in rm.iterrows():
        print(f"{n}. {r['risk']}: {r['level']} (L{r['likelihood']} x I{r['impact']} = {r['score']})")

How to read the matrix. Each numbered dot is a risk from the table, placed by likelihood (left to right) and impact (bottom to top); the background runs from green (low) to red (high). A filled dot means its likelihood was measured from our data; a white dot means it is the team's judgement.

What it shows. The highest risks are the ones our evaluation found directly: Claude over-using "limit or oppose", misreading long comments, and missing transparency arguments. Each of them has a matching safeguard in 12.4 (review of every "limit or oppose" label, the long-comment rule, and a caveat on the transparency share). The risks we could not measure (model updates, rubber-stamping reviewers) are controlled by process: revalidation triggers and checks on the reviewers.

12.6 Audit trail and shelf life¶

Class 18: an audit can answer what was asked, what came back, under which settings and who signed off, but not why the model answered as it did. Logging must be designed in from day one. This cell checks what our saved records actually contain.

In [46]:

What it shows. Every saved answer records the prompt version, the raw answer, the model, the settings, the token counts and the time it took, and the review queue records which safeguard fired. Two items are not recorded yet: a timestamp, and who ran and approved each batch; both should be added before production use (see 12.7).

What cannot be recorded, and our policy on it.

  • Why Claude chose a label. Its evidence quote and any reasoning are generated text, not a record of the computation. Escalation therefore never relies on asking the model to explain itself: a person reads the comment.
  • A faithful re-run. The API no longer accepts a temperature setting, and providers can update a model behind the same name. Saved answers are the record; a re-run is a new measurement (our stability test shows 90% of stances repeat exactly).

Shelf life. Every number in Section 8 was measured against claude-haiku-5-5 with prompt v2 on one date. "We validated it" expires: the gold-standard evaluation and the stability test must be re-run on any model or prompt change, or quarterly, whichever comes first, before results are reported again.

12.7 Governance recommendations and limitations¶

Recommendations: the operating rules for this workflow

  1. Keep a human in the loop for reporting. One governance check failed (long comments), so results are reported only with human review of the flagged comments. Automatic reporting is allowed only once every check passes on a fresh evaluation.
  2. Adopt the recommended review queue: low confidence OR quote not found OR over 200 words. On our data it catches 5 of 10 errors for 21% of comments, against 4 of 10 for the current queue; the cut-off is the lightest workload that catches the most errors within the 30% limit (12.1). Because it still misses half of Claude's errors, test a targeted extra rule next: review medium-confidence answers for comments that mention the FTC or the rule, the hardest type of comment.
  3. Never report the "limit or oppose" share without reviewing every comment in it. It is the worst category (12.3): most of Claude's labels there may be wrong, and the error points in one direction, overstating opposition to the FTC.
  4. Keep the 5% random audit and watch the reviewers. The audit detects drift in comments the queue never sees. If reviewers agree with Claude more than 98% of the time, check a sample of their decisions for rubber-stamping.
  5. Re-validate on a trigger, not a hunch. Re-run the gold-standard evaluation and the stability test on any model or prompt change, or quarterly. Investigate if stance F1 falls by more than the minimum detectable difference, or stability falls below 90%.
  6. Close the audit-trail gaps. Add a timestamp and the name of the person who ran and approved each batch to every saved answer.
  7. Improve the prompt where Claude struggles, then re-test. Add an explicit rule and example for "opposes the rule because they think it allows the practice", examples of indirect demands and implicit transparency arguments, and split long comments.
  8. Keep data rules strict. Send only comment text to the API, after name masking; keep the API key in .env; never send organizations' attachments or personal details from the docket metadata.

Limitations of this governance evidence

  • Thin evidence for rare categories and subgroups. The back-tests rest on 10 known errors, the length groups have only 2 to 5 errors each (the chi-square test is not significant), and the "mentions the rule" group has only 15 comments. Rates and ratios carry wide uncertainty: they show direction, not precise effects.
  • The gold standard was built by the two of us, who also wrote the coding dictionary; independent coders would be a stronger test.
  • Some likelihoods and all impacts are judgements. The risk matrix marks which likelihoods are measured and which are assumed.
  • The dollar figures rest on stated assumptions (estimated human time, $30 an hour, $5 per uncaught error) and can be changed in the code.
  • No demographic subgroups. Comments carry no reliable demographic information, so fairness is checked across types of comment, not types of commenter.
  • One model, one prompt, one date. Every number expires when the model or prompt changes.

13. Answers to the business questions¶

This section returns to the questions set out in Section 1 and answers each one from the evidence above. Every answer carries its status: validated (passed the governance thresholds), not validated (failed them; human review required), provisional (the hand-coded gold standard is not finished yet), or pending.

  • Questions 1–4 are about the workflow: can an organization rely on GenAI to analyze comments, at what cost, where does it fail, and under what controls?
  • Questions 5–6 are about the findings: what individual commenters object to and what they want the FTC to do, for companies that use personalized pricing.
In [47]:
# ANSWERS TO THE BUSINESS QUESTIONS (built from the results above)
# Returns to the six questions from Section 1 and answers each one in a
# sentence, using the numbers computed above. Each answer carries its status,
# and any question whose evidence is not ready yet says PENDING.

# Small helpers to format percentages and confidence intervals
def pct(x):
    return f"{x:.0%}"

def ci(lo, hi):
    return f"95% CI {lo:.0%}-{hi:.0%}"

answers = {}

# Q1. How accurately does an LLM classify comments compared with human coders?
# Claude's stance score and agreement with the gold standard, next to the
# human-human agreement and the best cheaper method.
if gold is None:
    answers["1. Accuracy vs human coders"] = "PENDING: needs the hand-coded gold standard (Section 8)."
else:
    sc = stance_scores.set_index("model")
    b, rs = sc.loc[BEST], reason_scores.set_index("model").loc[BEST]
    best_base = sc.drop(index=[m for m in sc.index if m.startswith("Claude")])["macro_f1"].idxmax()
    answers["1. Accuracy vs human coders"] = (
        f"{BEST} labels stance with judged macro-F1 {b['macro_f1']:.2f} (95% CI {b['f1_ci_low']:.2f}-{b['f1_ci_high']:.2f}) and "
        f"{pct(b['accuracy'])} accuracy; its agreement with the gold standard (kappa {b['kappa_vs_gold']:.2f}) compares with "
        f"human-human kappa {human_stance['kappa'].iloc[0]:.2f}. The best cheaper method ({best_base}) reaches "
        f"{sc.loc[best_base, 'macro_f1']:.2f}. Reasons: micro-F1 {rs['micro_f1']:.2f}. Status: stance {STATUS['stance']}, "
        f"reasons {STATUS['reasons']}.")

# Q2. What does it cost per comment compared with human analysts?
# Measured Claude cost and the projection to 100,000 comments (Section 11).
row = projection.set_index("comments").loc[100_000]
answers["2. Cost vs human analysts"] = (
    f"Measured cost: ${llm_cost_per_comment:.5f} per comment ({production_variant}). Labeling 100,000 comments would cost "
    f"about ${row['llm_cost_usd']:,.0f} with Claude, versus {row['human_hours']:,.0f} analyst hours (${row['human_cost_usd']:,.0f}) "
    f"by hand; with a {THRESHOLDS['audit_share']:.0%} human audit, about ${row['llm_plus_review_usd']:,.0f}. "
    f"Human time is estimated at {HUMAN_MINUTES_FOR_GOLD:.0f} minutes per coder for the {N_GOLD} gold comments, from their length (Section 11).")

# Q3. Where does it fail?
# The most common error, any comment-length group flagged, and stability.
if gold is None:
    answers["3. Where it fails"] = "PENDING: needs the gold standard to compare Claude's labels with."
else:
    top = pairs.index[0] if len(pairs) else None
    flagged = length_slices.index[length_slices["flag"]].tolist()
    answers["3. Where it fails"] = (
        (f"Most common stance error: gold '{top[0]}' labeled '{top[1]}' ({pairs.iloc[0]} of {N_GOLD} comments). " if top else "No stance errors. ")

# Q4. What controls make it safe to use?

# Print the answers, and check none is missing
for q, a in answers.items():
    print(f"{q}\n   {a}\n")
assert len(answers) == 6, "Every business question must have an answer or a PENDING note"

1. Accuracy vs human coders
   Claude zero-shot labels stance with judged macro-F1 0.93 (95% CI 0.86-0.97) and 90% accuracy; its agreement with the gold standard (kappa 0.82) compares with human-human kappa 0.95. The best cheaper method (TF-IDF + logistic regression) reaches 0.66. Reasons: micro-F1 0.78. Status: stance validated, reasons validated.

2. Cost vs human analysts
   Measured cost: $0.00028 per comment (zeroshot). Labeling 100,000 comments would cost about $28 with Claude, versus 1,305 analyst hours ($39,144) by hand; with a 5% human audit, about $1,985. Human time is estimated at 63 minutes per coder for the 80 gold comments, from their length (Section 11).

3. Where it fails
   Most common stance error: gold 'unclear' labeled 'limit_or_oppose_intervention' (3 of 80 comments). Error rate is disproportionately high for medium (16-50), long (>50). Stance was identical across 3 runs for 90% of comments. Errors are listed in coding/claude_stance_errors.csv.

4. Controls needed
   8 of 9 governance checks passed; failed: Worst length-group error ratio. Automatic reporting is NOT allowed. 256 comments (16%) go to human review (low confidence, invalid answer, or quote not found), plus a 5% random audit of every run.

5. What commenters object to
   the price difference: 49% (95% CI 46%-51%); the use of their data: 50% (95% CI 47%-52%); the lack of disclosure: 10% (95% CI 9%-11%). Fairness and consumer harm: 48%. A comment can give several reasons. Status: validated.

6. What commenters want the FTC to do
   Part A (the policy): stronger action than proposed: 65% (95% CI 63%-67%); support as proposed: 2%; mixed or conditional: 1%; limit or oppose: 2%; unclear: 30%. Part B (the practice): at least 67% are against personalized pricing, no stance defends it, and 60% of those who did not say what should happen still give an objection to it. Status: validated.

What this means¶

For organizations adopting GenAI to analyze public comments (regulators, law firms, public-affairs teams), Questions 1–4:

  • GenAI is a strong first-pass reader, not a replacement for analysts. In our run Claude zero-shot matched the hand-coded gold standard on stance with macro-F1 0.93 and kappa 0.82 (humans agreed with each other at kappa 0.95), far above sentiment (0.43), topics (0.56) and a trained TF-IDF classifier (0.66). Its value is concentrating human attention: it labels every comment for a fraction of a cent and routes the uncertain ones (about 16%) to people.
  • It fails in predictable places. Errors rise with comment length (21% on long comments vs 4% on short ones), it sometimes reads anger at personalized pricing as opposition to the FTC (it predicted limit or oppose 5 times for 1 real case), and it misses some transparency arguments. Its own confidence rating predicts its errors, which is what makes a review queue work.
  • Validation is the real cost. Running the model on 1,566 comments cost about $0.44; building the human gold standard and checking the model against it is where the time goes, and it must be repeated when the model, prompt or topic changes.
  • Controls must be measurable. 8 of 9 governance checks passed; the length check failed, so results are reported only together with human review of the flagged comments.

For companies that use personalized pricing (retailers, platforms, travel and ride-sharing firms), Questions 5–6:

  • Disclosure alone is unlikely to defuse public opposition. About two thirds of individual commenters (65%) want stronger action than the FTC proposed, typically a ban, while under 2% support the proposal as it stands and under 3% want less regulation (and that last figure is probably overstated, see Section 8.4).
  • The objection is to data use and unequal prices, not to secrecy. Personal-data use (50%), the price difference itself (49%) and fairness (48%) dominate; lack of disclosure is cited by only about 10%. Companies relying on "we disclosed it" as their defense may be misreading where public pressure is heading.
  • These are commenters, not the public. People who comment are self-selected and more likely to hold strong views, so these shares indicate the direction of regulatory pressure, not public opinion as a whole.

    "scikit-learn": sklearn.__version__, "scipy": scipy.__version__, "anthropic": anthropic.__version__,
    "seed": SEED, "model": LLM_MODEL, "sampling": SAMPLING, "effort": EFFORT, "prompt_version": PROMPT_VERSION,
    "comments_analyzed": len(df), "pilot": N_PILOT, "gold": N_GOLD, "coders": ", ".join(CODERS),
    "data_file_sha256": hashlib.sha256(DATA_FILE.read_bytes()).hexdigest()[:16],
}
for k, v in record.items():
    print(f"{k}: {v}")

15. Save results for the Streamlit app¶

The app (app.py) shows this workflow interactively, organised by Understand, Use, Evaluate and Govern. So that it never recalculates or retypes a number, this cell saves every result it needs to outputs/app/app_results.json, together with the exact prompt and model settings, so the app's live classifier behaves exactly like this notebook.

In [49]:
# SAVE RESULTS FOR THE STREAMLIT APP
# Writes the evaluation, findings, governance and cost results to one JSON
# file. The app reads only this file plus the saved labels, so the numbers
# in the app always match this notebook.
APP_DIR = ROOT / "outputs" / "app"
APP_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# 1. Helper: turn a table into a list of rows that JSON can store
def rows(table, index_name=None):
    t = table.reset_index() if index_name is None else table.rename_axis(index_name).reset_index()
    return json.loads(t.to_json(orient="records"))

if gold is None or labels_all is None:
    print("PENDING: the app needs the gold standard and the production run.")
else:
    # 2. McNemar p-value for zero-shot vs few-shot (recomputed here so it can be saved)
    from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import mcnemar
    z_ok = stance_merged["Claude zero-shot"]["pred"].values == stance_merged["Claude zero-shot"]["gold"].values
    f_ok = stance_merged["Claude few-shot"]["pred"].values == stance_merged["Claude few-shot"]["gold"].values
    mcnemar_p = mcnemar([[(z_ok & f_ok).sum(), (z_ok & ~f_ok).sum()], [(~z_ok & f_ok).sum(), (~z_ok & ~f_ok).sum()]], exact=True).pvalue

    # 3. Confusion matrix of the chosen Claude version (rows = gold, columns = Claude)
    m = stance_merged[BEST]
    cm = confusion_matrix(m["gold"], m["pred"], labels=STANCE_LABELS)

    results = {
        # Settings, prompt and dictionary, so the live classifier matches the notebook
        "settings": {"model": LLM_MODEL, "effort": EFFORT, "max_output_tokens": MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS, "prompt_version": PROMPT_VERSION,
                     "price_in_per_mtok": PRICE_IN_PER_MTOK, "price_out_per_mtok": PRICE_OUT_PER_MTOK, "seed": SEED,
                     "best": BEST, "best_variant": BEST_VARIANT, "system_prompt": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        "dictionary": {"stance": STANCE, "reasons": {k: v[0] for k, v in REASONS.items()}},
        "thresholds": THRESHOLDS,
        # Understand / Use: the data
        "data": {"comments": len(df), "docket_total": DOCKET_TOTAL, "median_words": float(df["n_words"].median()),
                 "mean_words": float(df["n_words"].mean()), "near_duplicates": int(df["is_near_duplicate"].sum()),
                 "duplicate_groups": int(df.loc[df["is_near_duplicate"], "dup_group"].nunique()),
                 "vader": df["vader_label"].astype(str).value_counts(normalize=True).to_dict(),
                 "topics": df["topic_name"].value_counts(normalize=True).to_dict(),
                 "ban_topics": [TOPIC_NAMES[k] for k in BAN_TOPIC_IDS]},
        # Evaluate
        "human": {"stance": rows(human_stance), "reasons": rows(human_reasons), "mean_jaccard": float(mean_jac)},
        "stance_scores": rows(stance_scores.set_index("model")),
        "stance_per_class": rows(stance_per_class.set_index("model")),
        "confusion": {"labels": STANCE_LABELS, "matrix": cm.tolist()},
        "mcnemar_p": float(mcnemar_p),
        "mdd": rows(mdd_tab.set_index("comparison")), "mdd_single": float(mdd_single),
        "reason_scores": rows(reason_scores.set_index("model")),
        "reason_per_class": rows(reason_per_class.set_index("model")),
        "stability": float(stability),
        "length_slices": rows(length_slices, "length"),
        "confidence_errors": rows(by_conf, "confidence"),
        "errors": [{"comment_id": r.comment_id, "text": mask_names(r.text), "gold": r.stance_gold, "claude": r.stance_claude,
                    "confidence": r.confidence, "quote": r.evidence_quote} for r in wrong.itertuples()],
        # Use: findings
        "stance_tab": rows(stance_tab, "stance"), "practice_tab": rows(practice_tab, "group"),
        "unsaid_evidence": unsaid_evidence.to_dict(), "reason_tab": rows(reason_tab, "reason"),
        "reasons_by_stance": rows(assoc.set_index("reason")),
        # Govern
        "governance": rows(governance.set_index("check")),
        "review_counts": {k: int(v) for k, v in flags.sum().items()}, "review_total": int(len(review)),
        "audit_total": int(len(audit)),
        # Cost
        "cost_per_variant": rows(per_variant, "variant"), "projection": rows(projection.set_index("comments")),
        "total_api_cost": float(logs["cost_usd"].sum()), "llm_cost_per_comment": float(llm_cost_per_comment),
        "llm_seconds_per_comment": float(llm_seconds_per_comment), "human_minutes_for_gold": float(HUMAN_MINUTES_FOR_GOLD),
        "status": STATUS, "record": record,
    }

    # 4. Write the file and check it can be read back
    out_file = APP_DIR / "app_results.json"
    out_file.write_text(json.dumps(results, indent=1, default=str), encoding="utf-8")
    assert json.loads(out_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["data"]["comments"] == len(df)
    print(f"Saved results for the app -> {out_file.relative_to(ROOT)} ({out_file.stat().st_size / 1024:.0f} KB)")
    print("Start the app from the repo folder with:  streamlit run app.py")
